summary: Photosynthesis for 11–12 year-olds: establish the word equation (carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, driven by light energy captured by chlorophyll), source each input to its origin (CO₂ from air via stomata, water and minerals from soil via roots, light to the canopy), distinguish reactants from products, and explain why nearly all life depends on photosynthesis for food/biomass and atmospheric oxygen. Core misconception to confront: that plants get their food/mass from the soil. Also establish that plants both photosynthesise and respire. The target teaching objective is an input→output process where learners vary each raw material and observe the plant's response; labelling/sorting and reading-based experiment work are complementary scaffolds and assessments.
misconceptions: Believing plants get their food from the soil, or that soil minerals ARE the plant's food — minerals are needed in tiny amounts for making proteins/chlorophyll; the bulk food (glucose) is built from CO₂ and water.
Thinking plants photosynthesise instead of respiring, or that they only respire at night — plants respire continuously; photosynthesis is additional and light-dependent.
Assuming chlorophyll is a reactant that gets used up, rather than a catalyst-like pigment that captures light and is not consumed.
Confusing which gas is taken in and which is given out (mixing up the CO₂-in / O₂-out of photosynthesis with the reverse in respiration).
Thinking glucose is stored and used as glucose only — not realising it is converted to starch for storage and used to build the plant's biomass (cellulose, proteins).

activities.title: Feed the plant: vary each input and watch the response
steps: Work with a plant model (physical bench setup, a simulation, or a teacher-run demonstration) that has three controllable supplies: a light source (brightness), air/CO₂, and water from the soil.

Starting with all three supplies on, raise each one in turn and observe and record what happens to the rate of oxygen bubbling (and, in a simulation, the displayed amount of glucose being built; glucose cannot be watched directly on a real bench).
Set water and CO₂ to maximum, then switch the light OFF. Predict first, then observe: does the plant keep making food? Write down what this tells you about which input drives the process.

In the simulation or model, switch each remaining input to zero one at a time and record whether photosynthesis stalls, concluding which inputs are necessary (in a real plant, cutting off water or CO₂ slows photosynthesis gradually rather than switching it off instantly).
Leave the plant in the dark and reveal/consider the plant's own use of oxygen; state in a sentence why this shows plants also respire, not only photosynthesise.
activities.insight: Light energy is the driver of photosynthesis and each of CO₂, water and light is necessary; glucose is built by the plant from air and water, and plants respire (use oxygen) as well as photosynthesise.

activities.title: van Helmont's willow: predict where the mass comes from
steps: Read/consider the classic experiment: a small willow is planted in a weighed pot of soil and watered for about five years until it gains many kilograms, while the soil loses only a tiny fraction of that (in the usual account, about 2 ounces, roughly 57 g).
Before the result is revealed, predict how much soil mass will be lost and, importantly, explain WHY.
Compare your predicted reason with the result: the soil barely changed, so the tree's large mass gain cannot have come mainly from the soil.

State in your own words where nearly all the extra mass (the wood) actually comes from. Explain that the experiment shows it did not come mainly from the soil (van Helmont himself concluded it came from water), and that later evidence showed the carbon comes from carbon dioxide in the air.
Answer follow-up probes: What happens to a well-watered plant kept in total darkness and why? Which part of the carbon dioxide ends up in the wood? Does a plant need oxygen, and when?
Extend to a sealed sunny greenhouse: predict what would happen to the measured CO₂ inside during the day, and explain why.
activities.insight: Almost all of a plant's extra mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air combined with water, using light energy; soil supplies water and small amounts of minerals, not the bulk of the mass.

activities.title: Name and source the parts: leaf anatomy and input origins
steps: On a whole-plant diagram, draw or place arrows showing CO₂ entering leaves, water and minerals rising from roots, and light striking the leaf canopy.
Label a leaf cross-section with stomata (gas in/out), chloroplasts (where light is captured), and veins (bringing water).

Sort a set of items — {carbon dioxide, water, minerals, glucose, oxygen} — into reactants of photosynthesis, products of photosynthesis, or neither (minerals are needed by the plant but are not reactants in the photosynthesis word equation). Then sort only the materials the plant takes in (carbon dioxide, water, minerals) into from-air vs from-soil, noting that glucose and oxygen are made by the plant.

Explain, in a lift-the-flap or written response, the myth 'the plant eats the soil': state that the plant builds its food from carbon dioxide from the air and water, using light energy, and that the soil supplies water and small amounts of minerals, not the bulk of the food.
activities.insight: The leaf is the 'factory' where carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil are turned into glucose and oxygen using light energy captured by chlorophyll; reactants and products can be named and correctly attributed to their origin.

activities.title: Pairing photosynthesis with respiration
steps: After the word equation is secure, write photosynthesis and respiration as paired processes, noting respiration broadly reverses the gas exchange (uses oxygen, releases carbon dioxide).
Explain when each happens: photosynthesis only in light; respiration continuously, day and night.
Answer: does a plant respire at night? Does it respire during the day? Justify your answer.

Connect to the wider picture: explain in a sentence why nearly all life on Earth depends on photosynthetic organisms for food/biomass and for maintaining atmospheric oxygen, foreshadowing the carbon cycle (photosynthesis is a route by which CO₂ leaves the atmosphere).
activities.insight: Plants both photosynthesise and respire; photosynthesis builds glucose and releases oxygen, respiration releases glucose's stored energy and uses oxygen, and together these underpin life's dependence on photosynthesis.

activities.title: Observe a real phenomenon: oxygen from pondweed and the starch test
steps: Observe pondweed (such as Elodea) under a lamp: count or compare the rate of gas bubbles (mostly oxygen) rising as the lamp is moved closer or further away, keeping the water temperature steady (e.g. use an LED lamp or a heat shield) so that light is the only factor changed.
Describe what happens to the bubbling as the light gets brighter, and relate it to the word equation (oxygen is a product).

Consider or observe a destarched leaf tested with iodine after partial covering: the leaf turns blue-black only where light reached, showing starch (made from glucose) formed only where photosynthesis occurred — which also shows glucose is stored as starch rather than kept only as glucose.
Write a short conclusion linking each observation to which input was being varied and what it shows.
activities.insight: The abstract equation is grounded in observable evidence: oxygen is released as a product and its rate responds to light, and the products of photosynthesis (stored as starch) appear only where light reached.

checkQuestion: A tree grows from a tiny seed into something that weighs many tonnes. Where does nearly all of that extra material — the wood, the mass — actually come from? Explain how you know.
checkAnswer: Almost all the extra mass comes from carbon dioxide taken from the AIR, combined with water, using light energy captured by chlorophyll to make glucose (carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen); the soil supplies water and small amounts of mineral nutrients, not the bulk of the mass.
